### PART VI — Multivariate Methods & Reproducible Practice · Modules 15–16

*a taste of multivariate statistics · reproducible statistical practice*

Read a section, then do the matching exercises in `PartVI_exercises.R` before continuing.

## Where Part VI takes you

Two final pieces complete a modern biostatistics toolkit. **Multivariate methods** (Module 15) handle the common situation where you measure many variables at once — several traits, many genes, whole communities — and want to see structure across all of them together. **Reproducible practice** (Module 16) is the set of habits — power analysis, multiple-testing correction, honest reporting, reproducible code — that make the difference between statistics that hold up and statistics that don’t replicate. The techniques in Parts I–V are necessary; these habits are what make them trustworthy.

**Time guide.** Module 15 ≈ 6h · Module 16 ≈ 5h. Total ≈ 11 hours. Datasets: `flower_traits.csv`, and any from earlier parts.

## Module 15 — A taste of multivariate statistics

Estimated: 6 hours. When each observation has many measurements, you cannot eyeball all the pairwise relationships. Multivariate methods summarise the joint structure — reducing dimensions, finding groups, and revealing gradients.

### 15.1 Why multivariate?

Measure four floral traits on 100 flowers and you have a 100×4 cloud you can’t fully plot. Multivariate methods answer: Which traits vary together? Do the flowers fall into natural groups? Can a few combined axes capture most of the variation? These are everyday questions in morphometrics, ecology (community data), and genomics (expression across thousands of genes).

### 15.2 Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

PCA finds new axes — **principal components** — that are combinations of your variables, ordered so the first captures the most variance, the second the most of what’s left, and so on. It reduces many correlated variables to a few informative axes.

    flow <- read.csv("data/flower_traits.csv")
    X <- flow[, c("petal_length_cm","petal_width_cm","sepal_length_cm","sepal_width_cm")]
    pca <- prcomp(X, scale. = TRUE)      # ALWAYS scale when variables have different units
    summary(pca)                          # variance explained by each PC

**Scaling matters:** `scale. = TRUE` standardises each variable to unit variance, so a trait measured in large numbers doesn’t dominate purely because of its units. For these flowers, PC1 captures ≈ 51% and PC2 ≈ 36% of the variation — together ≈ 87%, so a 2-D plot of PC1 vs PC2 represents the four traits almost completely.

    scores <- as.data.frame(pca$x)
    scores$species <- flow$species
    library(ggplot2)
    ggplot(scores, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = species)) + geom_point()   # the ordination plot
    pca$rotation                          # loadings: how each trait contributes to each PC

The **scores** place each flower in the new space (reveal grouping); the **loadings** (`rotation`) tell you what each axis *means* biologically — which traits drive PC1. Interpreting the loadings is the real skill.

### 15.3 Clustering

Where PCA finds continuous axes, **clustering** assigns observations to discrete groups.

    # hierarchical clustering
    d  <- dist(scale(X))                  # distances between flowers (scaled)
    hc <- hclust(d, method = "ward.D2")
    plot(hc)                              # a dendrogram
    groups <- cutree(hc, k = 4)           # cut into 4 clusters

    # k-means (you choose k)
    km <- kmeans(scale(X), centers = 4)
    km$cluster

**Hierarchical clustering** builds a tree (dendrogram) you cut at a chosen height; **k-means** partitions into a pre-set number of clusters. Both need a sensible distance and scaled variables. Clustering is **exploratory** — it will always return groups, whether or not real ones exist, so validate against known structure (here, species) and treat the groups as hypotheses, not facts.

### 15.4 Where multivariate fits in biology

PCA and clustering are the entry points to a large field: ordination methods (PCoA, NMDS) for ecological community data, discriminant analysis for classification, and the dimension-reduction steps (PCA, UMAP) that precede most single-cell and expression analyses. The two ideas here — *reduce to informative axes* and *find groups* — carry through all of it.

## Module 16 — Reproducible statistical practice

Estimated: 5 hours. The habits that make statistics trustworthy. None is hard; together they are what separate work that replicates from work that doesn’t.

### 16.1 Plan the sample size before the study

The most consequential statistical decision is made before any data exist: how many samples? An underpowered study wastes effort and, worse, produces unreliable “significant” results that exaggerate effects. Do a **power analysis** at the design stage:

    power.t.test(delta = 0.7, sd = 1.2, power = 0.8)        # n for a target effect
    power.anova.test(groups = 3, between.var = ..., within.var = ..., power = 0.8)

You specify the smallest effect worth detecting, the expected variability, and the power you want (80% is conventional); it returns the required n. Designing for power is cheaper than discovering afterwards that the study couldn’t have found anything.

### 16.2 The multiple-testing problem

Every test at α = 0.05 has a 5% false-positive rate. Run 20 tests on null data and you expect one “significant” result by chance; run 20,000 (a genomics screen) and you expect 1,000. Correct for it:

    p <- c(0.001, 0.01, 0.03, 0.04, 0.20)
    p.adjust(p, method = "bonferroni")     # controls the chance of ANY false positive (strict)
    p.adjust(p, method = "BH")             # controls the false DISCOVERY rate (Benjamini-Hochberg)

-   **Bonferroni** controls the family-wise error rate (any false positive) — strict, for a few critical tests.
-   **Benjamini–Hochberg (FDR)** controls the *proportion* of false positives among your “discoveries” — the right choice for large screens (differential expression, GWAS), where some false positives are acceptable if controlled.

Reporting raw p-values from a large screen without correction is one of the most common serious errors in computational biology.

### 16.3 Avoiding p-hacking and HARKing

Two subtler traps:

-   **p-hacking** — trying many analyses, variables, or subgroups and reporting only what reached p \< 0.05. This guarantees false positives. Decide your main analysis in advance; label anything else exploratory.
-   **HARKing** (Hypothesising After Results are Known) — presenting a pattern you found by chance as if you’d predicted it. Confirmatory and exploratory findings have different evidential weight; keep them labelled as such.

The defence is **pre-specification**: write down the main question, the analysis, and the sample size before collecting data (a pre-registration, even an informal one). It is the single strongest guard against fooling yourself.

### 16.4 Report effect sizes and uncertainty, not just p

The recurring theme of the course, as a rule: **report the estimated effect size with a confidence interval, not a p-value alone.** “Treatment increased growth by 7.6 cm (95% CI \[5.9, 9.3\])” is informative and honest; “the effect was significant (p \< 0.001)” is neither. Give the direction, the magnitude, the precision, and the units — then the p-value as a supporting detail if you wish.

### 16.5 Reproducible analysis in R

The computational half of trustworthiness:

-   **Script everything.** No manual steps, no spreadsheet edits — the path from raw data to result lives in code anyone can re-run.
-   **Use a reproducible report** (R Markdown / Quarto — companion R course, Part V): prose, code, and output in one document that regenerates from the data, so every number and figure is traceable.
-   **Set seeds** (`set.seed()`) for anything random, so simulations and bootstraps reproduce exactly.
-   **Record your environment** — R and package versions (`sessionInfo()`), ideally pinned with `renv` — so the analysis still runs next year.
-   **Share data and code.** Reproducibility by others is the ultimate test, and increasingly a requirement.

### 16.6 Where the course leaves you

You can now take a biological question from design to answer: choose a sound design and avoid pseudoreplication; describe and visualise data honestly; reason with probability and confidence intervals; test hypotheses and read p-values correctly; fit and check linear, generalised, and mixed models; explore multivariate structure; and do all of it reproducibly, reporting effect sizes with their uncertainty. That is applied biostatistics — not a bag of tests, but a disciplined way of learning from biological data.
